title: Shrinking slices: dilution on repeat

facts.label: Price
facts.value: 0.09 USD (simulated), after a 1-for-15 reverse split last quarter

facts.label: Shares outstanding
facts.value: Adjusted for the 1-for-20 split: 50 million three years ago → 180 million → 600 million before the latest 1-for-15 split (40 million after it)

facts.label: Revenue trend
facts.value: Small and flat: about 0.4 million USD a year for three years

facts.label: Cash
facts.value: Enough for about 4 months at the current rate of spending, according to its latest report

facts.label: Financing
facts.value: Loans that convert into new shares at a discount to the market price

facts.label: Filings and disclosures
facts.value: Filed on time; reports describe one product in early testing

question: Which of these are warning signs?

signs.text: The split-adjusted share count went from 50 million to 600 million in three years.
signs.explanation: That is 12 times as many shares. Someone who owned 1% of the split-adjusted shares (500,000) at the start would own about 0.083% before the latest split, unless they kept buying.

signs.text: Two reverse splits in two years.
signs.explanation: One reverse split proves little. Repeated ones, each after heavy dilution, suggest a cycle of issuing shares, the price sinking, and the split resetting it.

signs.text: Cash covers only about 4 months of spending.
signs.explanation: With little revenue, the company will likely need to raise more money soon, and recent history suggests that means more new shares.

signs.text: Loans convert into shares at a discount to the market price.
signs.explanation: Lenders can receive shares cheaply and sell them, which can push the price down and add more dilution. Worth reading the terms closely.
A good sign for transparency. The problem here is not hidden information but what the information shows.

signs.text: There is no sign of paid promotion.
signs.explanation: Also a good sign. Not every struggling small company is a pump and dump; some are real businesses running out of money.

signs.text: The company is working on a product in early testing.
signs.explanation: Not a warning sign. Many small companies are early-stage. But an early product does not pay today's bills.

investigate: Read the terms of the convertible loans: the discount, any limits, and how many shares could be created.
Check how many new shares the company is allowed to issue without asking shareholders.
Work out the cash runway yourself from the latest report: cash divided by monthly spending.
List every share issue and reverse split over the last few years, with dates.
Ask what has to go right for existing shareholders to benefit, given the likely future dilution.
verdict: This company looks open about its situation, with no promotion and on-time filings, but the situation itself is the risk: repeated dilution, repeated reverse splits, a short cash runway and discounted convertible loans. Even if the product succeeds, existing holders may own a much smaller slice by then. For a learner, staying out is the sensible decision until the financing problem is clearly solved.
